body.text: Recently, our Georgetown team has been inundated with media requests for commentary on allegations involving the exposure of Nvidia chip technology and the implications for U.S. national security. These inquiries typically focus on how China’s intelligence services conduct espionage and what can be done to counter them.

We do not discount this threat. Espionage, cyber intrusions, and other clandestine activities are longstanding features of China’s efforts to acquire foreign technology. But our research over more than a decade suggests that these activities account for only a fraction of China’s overall foreign technology acquisition effort – probably not the largest fraction, and arguably not the most consequential.

Rather, China has created a whole-of-nation ecosystem that operates through a combination of legal transactions, illicit activities, and what we call “extralegal” transfers: arrangements whose details are unavailable to outside observers and whose legality cannot readily be established.

Because these less visible practices lack the sensational appeal of conventional espionage, they rarely receive comparable attention. The result is a distorted public understanding of China’s technology acquisition system and a misallocation of the resources intended to counter it.
Beyond Conventional Espionage

China’s pursuit of foreign technology is neither new nor mysterious. Since the founding of the People’s Republic in 1949, Beijing has operated an elaborate infrastructure for identifying foreign technological advances, accessing them, and adapting them for domestic use.

The enterprise includes government ministries, scientific research institutions, commercial entities, technology transfer centers, professional associations, overseas laboratories, and programs designed to recruit scientists and engineers with specialized expertise.

Its antecedents extend further back, to China’s 19th-century efforts to acquire Western technology while preserving its domestic political and social institutions. Successive Chinese governments have formalized these efforts. The objective is not simply to copy inventions, but to leverage the knowledge to produce commercially and strategically useful results.
For analytical purposes, we distinguish among three broad categories of foreign technology acquisition.

Legal transfers include purchases of technology, foreign company acquisitions, joint research, investments in startups, overseas laboratories, university collaborations, and the recruitment of scientific personnel. These transactions are not inherently improper. Yet a transaction can be legal while also being a strategic risk.

Illegal transfers include traditional espionage, cyber theft, violations of nondisclosure agreements, theft of trade secrets, alleged “honey pot” operations, and other activities prohibited by law. These are the practices most familiar to the public, which media queries most frequently address – as in the case of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Extralegal transfers involve arrangements in which foreign technical knowledge is conveyed through channels that are not necessarily illegal but frequently opaque. Examples are undisclosed research affiliations, subsidized consulting, dual appointments, and the work of intermediaries whose relationships with China’s government are not apparent.

These categories are not exclusive. An otherwise legitimate collaboration may involve undisclosed conflicts of interest, while a commercial acquisition may be entirely lawful yet raise significant national security concerns.
Our concern is that the second category attracts disproportionate attention, while the first and third may facilitate transfers of equal or greater strategic consequence.
The Machinery Behind the Transfers
The scale and institutional character of China’s acquisition efforts distinguish them from isolated acts of industrial espionage.

One component is China’s science and technology intelligence (科技情报, STI) system. This network collects, analyzes, and distributes foreign technical information to domestic research and industrial organizations. Its civilian institutions include the Institute of Scientific and Technical Information of China, complemented by specialized organizations serving particular industries and defense requirements.

Another component is the ubiquitous “talent programs” – a network of organizations that identify and recruit overseas technical expertise. Chinese national and local authorities have sponsored numerous programs offering research funding, salaries, laboratory facilities, and other incentives to scientists and engineers working abroad.

Some arrangements involve permanent relocation to subsidized “commercialization centers.” Others permit researchers to maintain positions overseas while executing projects or consulting assignments in China. These include so-called “dual-base” (两个基地) arrangements, through which an individual may sustain professional activities in two countries.

Participation in such programs or in their global analogs – the Sino-U.S. (or Japanese, German, etc.) “professional associations” – does not by itself establish misconduct. That depends on the nature of the work, the information transferred, and whether participants comply with applicable disclosure requirements and contractual obligations.

Unlike a clandestine intelligence operation, much of this infrastructure is publicly acknowledged in Chinese government documents and institutional announcements. Its strategic significance lies not in secrecy alone, but in its organization, persistence, and cumulative effects.
Our research on China’s access to foreign artificial intelligence (AI) technology provides an instructive example.

China’s 2017 New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan explicitly encouraged cooperation with foreign universities and research institutions, the recruitment of international AI specialists, overseas mergers and acquisitions, venture capital investment, and the establishment of research facilities abroad.

Subsequent initiatives promoted international academic exchanges, joint laboratories, and other mechanisms for accessing foreign expertise. These are not clandestine activities; they are stated elements of Chinese national technology policy.

Our 2019 CSET study, “China’s Access to Foreign AI Technology,” found that the principal mechanisms supporting foreign AI acquisition were not necessarily illegal. We also concluded that many such transfers were poorly monitored and that the United States lacked sufficient information to assess their aggregate consequences.
The Danger of Looking Only for Spies

The problem is not that U.S. counterintelligence and law enforcement agencies have exaggerated the importance of Chinese espionage. Their investigations have exposed serious threats to U.S. technological and economic security. But successful investigations can create a misleading impression of the overall threat because criminal cases are visible, measurable, and newsworthy. Legal and extralegal transfers are harder to identify, much less quantify.

This distortion has practical consequences. Measures designed to prevent the theft of classified information or proprietary technology will not necessarily address transfers occurring through legitimate research, investment, or commercial relationships.

A related danger is treating Chinese students, scientists, or Americans of Chinese ancestry as presumptive security risks. Such generalizations are unjustified, undermine useful cooperation, and can damage the United States’ ability to attract and retain needed talent.

Recognizing the full scope of China’s technology acquisition system does not imply that the United States should retreat from international scientific cooperation or attempt to prevent all technology flows to China. It does, however, suggest several priorities.

First, investments in counterintelligence should be complemented by sustained open-source research into China’s technology policies, transfer organizations, recruitment programs, commercial investments, and research relationships.

Second, research institutions and companies should have clearer guidance on disclosure obligations and the protection of sensitive research. Transparency is a more practical starting point than blanket restrictions on international collaboration.

Third and most importantly, protecting U.S. technology cannot substitute for developing it. Sustained investment in research, education, and infrastructure is the best way to sustain American technological competitiveness.

The latest allegations involving semiconductor technology deserve serious investigation. Where wrongdoing is established, legal remedies should follow. But individual espionage cases are not an adequate guide to the scale or character of China’s efforts to acquire foreign technology. The strategic challenge is China’s system for acquiring foreign technology, not merely the spies. Until U.S. policymakers and the public recognize that distinction, we are prosecuting only the most visible part of a problem whose larger dimensions remain poorly understood.
